name: かいてん寿し 大倉 (Kaiten Sushi Okura)

claims.text: A traditional sushi counter where wheat-based soy sauce and seasoned sushi rice are used throughout; cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable and no gluten-free handling is documented.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (containing wheat) is the default condiment at the sushi counter.
All preparation centers on raw fish and shellfish at a shared sushi counter; any non-seafood item would share surfaces and tools with seafood.

name: Kamuna (しぜんおやつ工房カムナ)

claims.text: Owner intentionally bakes spelt wheat (スペルト小麦/古代小麦) on some Sundays in the same small kitchen: 「日曜日のみ不定期で『スペルト小麦（古代小麦）』を使用した『小麦に感謝の日』を開催いたします」. Spelt is wheat/gluten; shared-equipment cross-contact is a real, uncontrolled risk.
No wheat-free-kitchen claim, no 'may contain' warning and no cross-contact protocol are published. Absence of a warning is not evidence of safety.
Sweets shop; no soy sauce noted. Other allergens present: egg, butter (dairy), sesame, almond, cocoa, matcha.
Not vegan — egg is used for leavening and butter for dairy; no plant-based separation.
No published allergy-handling policy; owner reachable via Instagram @kamuna357 / LINE for questions.
Most days' products are rice-flour/mochi-flour based (Ishikawa 無農薬米粉), additive-free with reduced/no white sugar.
Owner is health-focused (former nurse) and transparent about when wheat is used.

name: 金沢茶屋 割烹つづみ (Kanazawa Chaya Kappo Tsuzumi)

claims.text: Signature jibuni is coated in wheat flour and the cuisine is soy-sauce and dashi based; wheat and gluten are pervasive across the menu.
Kaga cuisine here relies on standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) and soy-based seasonings; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
Dishes center on seafood, eel, fugu, duck, and wagyu with fish/meat-based dashi, so plant items would share animal-based stocks and prep.

name: 金澤ななほしカレー (Kanazawa Nanahoshi Curry)

claims.text: The shop is explicitly oriented toward dietary needs, stating it wants to serve diners of every food style, with a dedicated five-pungent-free bean curry for vegetarian/vegan/macrobiotic/Muslim guests.
All curries are made with no wheat flour and no sugar, making the core dishes inherently gluten-free rather than relying on a single modified menu item.
Offers a dairy-free, gluten-free, plant-based cacao-and-nut vegan curry alongside the five-pungent-free bean curry.
The curry is described as additive-free and oil-light (no-oil/ノンオイル, 無添加 in the shop's own positioning), aimed at being easy on the stomach.

name: 金沢おでん 地酒地魚 新近江町商店 (Kanazawa Oden Jizake Jizakana Shin-Omicho Sh)

claims.text: Kanazawa oden is simmered as a shared pot with wheat-based fish cakes and other items, so broth and ingredients are not gluten-free and share cooking surfaces with other dishes.
Regional dishes (sushi, sashimi, oden, rice bowls) are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no gluten-free tamari is documented.
The kitchen is built around seafood, fish dashi, and Noto beef; oden broth is fish-based, so even vegetable items would share fish/meat broth and surfaces.
Touchscreen ordering at every seat shows item names and prices, helping diners review what they are ordering, and English menus are available.

name: 金沢和食 みんなのまなぶ (Kanazawa Washoku Minna no Manabu)

claims.text: No gluten-free handling is documented; fried dishes such as crab cream croquette are on the menu, implying shared frying and breading with wheat.
Traditional Kanazawa washoku relying on soy sauce and dashi seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and no GF substitute is mentioned.
Dashi (typically fish/bonito based) and fresh seafood are central to the cooking, so animal products pervade the menu.
Traditional Kaga cuisine relies on wheat-based soy sauce and dashi in simmered and braised dishes such as jibuni; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
Menu is seafood- and meat-forward (grilled fish, snow crab, jibuni stew) with fish/kombu dashi throughout; no vegan offerings are documented.
Menu centers on tempura (wheat batter), soy-seasoned jibuni, and dashi-based dishes; no gluten-free handling is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.
Kaga dishes such as jibuni and accompanying sauces use Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat.
Cooking is built around fish, shellfish, meat and dashi; no vegan preparation or separation is documented.
